overview: The map uses “Berbers” for a vast North African area from about 1500 to 500 BCE. This broad later label should not imply one ancient nation, language or government. Archaeology reveals varied communities of farmers, herders and craftspeople. Named sites below show that diversity, with earlier and later examples clearly dated.

periods.title: The opening centuries of the map
periods.summary: These centuries fall within North Africa’s unevenly documented late prehistory, with differing local farming and herding traditions.

periods.title: Kach Kouch farming settlement
periods.summary: Houses and farming remains predate the local appearance of Phoenician imports.

periods.title: New connections
periods.summary: Kach Kouch residents combined established building techniques with new materials and Mediterranean connections.

periods.title: A later written witness
periods.summary: Dougga’s dedication to Massinissa belongs to the Numidian kingdom, centuries after this map window.

items.text: Long before this map window, Oued Beht in Morocco flourished around 3400 to 2900 BCE. Its main concentration of finds covers about nine to ten hectares. Numerous deep pits suggest substantial storage, though archaeologists are still testing how the site was organized.

At Oued Beht, charred barley, wheat and peas survived alongside wild olive and pistachio remains. Animal bones include goats, sheep, cattle and pigs. These scraps reveal the ingredients and animals around an early farming community without supplying an exact ancient recipe.

Oued Beht craftspeople made polished stone axes and adzes on site: unfinished examples and manufacturing flakes remain. Grinding stones helped process food, while pottery included storage jars, cooking vessels and decorated bowls. Skilled hands equipped both fields and kitchens.

North Africa’s environments changed as the Sahara became drier. Archaeological research finds varied responses, including durable herding traditions and farming in suitable areas. Movement with animals could be a successful way to use land where permanent cultivation was less practical.

sections.title: Households within the map’s ancient dates

items.text: At Kach Kouch in northern Morocco, postholes and clay wall fragments suggest rounded houses built from woven branches covered with earth. Larger central posts probably supported roofs. Between about 1300 and 900 BCE, families lived in a settled farming community.

Kach Kouch farmers grew barley, wheat, beans and peas. Later levels contain grapes and olives too. Bone tools probably served leatherworking, while sheep and goats dominate the identifiable animal remains. Food production and making useful things happened together.

In the eighth and seventh centuries BCE, one Kach Kouch building combined a rectangular stone base with older woven-branch and clay wall techniques. Its builders adapted incoming ideas to familiar methods: an ancient home improvement project with local expertise.

Farther east, Althiburos in Tunisia preserves early Numidian occupation from the tenth or ninth to the early seventh century BCE. Its farming economy included wheat, barley, lentils and peas, with grape and fig remains. North African households had distinct regional histories.

Althiburos animal bones show that sheep, goats, cattle and pigs mattered to its economy. Researchers examine bones alongside plant remains to understand how crop growing and keeping livestock fitted together, rather than treating the settlement as only a farming or only a herding place.

Even dung can be useful historical evidence. At Althiburos, microscopic plant particles and tiny mineral bodies from animal droppings helped researchers identify places where livestock waste accumulated. Archaeologists sometimes solve household mysteries with material nobody originally meant to preserve.

“MSNSN” is the scholarly transliteration of the ancient name Massinissa. A dedication at Dougga honours this Numidian king around 138 BCE, after the map’s ancient interval. Such names, compared across Libyan and Punic inscriptions, help scholars read otherwise difficult texts.

Libyco-Berber inscriptions use several related alphabets, often made from lines, circles and dots. Bilingual monuments at Dougga gave researchers matching personal names in Punic and Libyan. This was a vital clue, although many short inscriptions remain difficult to translate.

ending.text: The map’s 500 BCE endpoint does not mark a single collapse. Kach Kouch itself was abandoned around 600 BCE, apparently without violence. Regional societies kept changing; the Mauretanian kingdom emerged in subsequent centuries.
